Apex InsightAugust 29, 2026

Strong Where Rates Matter Least

Headline GDP, payroll momentum, and consumer expectations are softening, but private domestic demand, AI-linked investment, and hard-asset strength are making the policy signal far less straightforward.

Key Conclusions

  • Headline GDP is a weaker signal than usual because surging capital-goods imports can subtract from measured growth while private domestic demand remains firm.
  • The consumer and labor market are cooling beneath the surface, but the data still describe caution and stagnation more than a synchronized recessionary break.
  • July PCE and resilient private demand keep the Fed's burden of proof on disinflation, not simply on weaker housing, confidence, or payroll momentum.
  • Gold and Bitcoin rising together despite high real yields suggest investors are increasingly hedging the limits of how much long-end restraint policymakers can tolerate.
Opening Argument

The Composition of Growth Is Changing

The economy continues to resist a simple description of either strong or weak. Headline GDP has slowed, payroll growth has moved toward stall speed, consumer expectations remain depressed, and housing continues to absorb the effects of elevated long-term rates. Yet underneath those signals, private domestic demand remains considerably stronger, capital spending continues accelerating, and the AI investment cycle is generating enough demand for equipment that a growing portion must be satisfied through imports. The result is an economy where traditional cyclical indicators increasingly understate the strength of the capital-intensive portion of the expansion.

That divergence is becoming more important for both the Federal Reserve and markets. Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers are growing materially faster than headline GDP, while the widening trade deficit increasingly reflects surging capital-goods imports rather than collapsing domestic demand. At the same time, the labor market has become less dynamic without developing into a firing cycle. Payroll momentum has fallen dramatically, but declining labor-force participation is lowering the amount of job creation required to keep unemployment contained. The consumer remains functional, but expectations are deteriorating, underlying income excluding transfers is weak, and the savings rate is beginning to rise as households become more cautious.

The complication is inflation. July PCE did not provide the continued disinflation Kevin Warsh has increasingly made a prerequisite for patience. Six-month annualized PCE is running above the year-over-year rate, underlying inflation remains broad, and the private economy is still strong enough that financial conditions are difficult to characterize as universally restrictive. Warsh's Jackson Hole message therefore materially clarified the reaction function: weakness in housing, payroll growth, or confidence will not necessarily prevent additional tightening if inflation fails to move toward 2% at sufficient speed.

That leaves an unusual policy configuration heading into September. The Fed is attempting to restore inflation credibility at the front end while Treasury is becoming increasingly sensitive to pressure at the long end. Fiscal deficits remain large, term premium remains elevated, and policymakers have already demonstrated a willingness to intervene in Treasury-market structure when long-term financing costs become uncomfortable. The tension between those two objectives is increasingly visible across asset prices, particularly in the simultaneous strength of Gold and Bitcoin despite historically elevated real yields.

This week's report therefore focuses less on whether the economy is slowing and more on what is slowing, what continues accelerating, and how policymakers respond when those forces increasingly point in opposite directions.

GDP Composition

Headline GDP Is Understating Private Demand

The latest GDP and trade data provide another example of why the headline growth rate is becoming increasingly difficult to interpret without understanding what is happening underneath it. Nominal GDP increased 6.5% over the year through the second quarter while real GDP grew only 2.1%, leaving roughly a 4.4 percentage point gap attributable to the economy-wide price level. Put differently, a significant portion of the dollar growth businesses and households are experiencing continues to reflect higher prices rather than additional real output. That helps reconcile some of the disconnect between resilient nominal revenues, corporate earnings, and economic surveys on one side and considerably weaker household perceptions of the economy on the other. Businesses really are seeing more dollars flow through the economy, but those dollars are purchasing considerably less incremental real activity than the nominal numbers imply.

The chart below adds another important distinction by comparing Real GDP with Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers. The latter strips out inventories, government spending, and net exports to provide a cleaner read on underlying private domestic demand. The latest divergence is striking. Real GDP is running at roughly a 1.5% annualized pace while Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers are growing around 4.2%. In other words, the domestic private economy is currently considerably stronger than the headline GDP number suggests. That is important because a 1.5% GDP print viewed in isolation looks like an economy approaching stall speed. A 4%+ private-demand number tells a very different story.

One reason for that divergence is increasingly visible in the trade data. The July advance goods trade deficit widened sharply to roughly $119 billion as imports accelerated and exports declined. Imports subtract from GDP by construction, meaning a sufficiently large widening in the trade deficit can mechanically reduce measured economic growth even when those imports are being purchased because domestic demand is exceptionally strong. That accounting treatment is necessary because GDP measures production occurring within the United States rather than everything purchased by U.S. businesses and households. But it can create a misleading cyclical signal if the composition of imports is ignored.

Capital goods are the critical piece of the current move. Imports of capital equipment surged in July, with strength across computers, semiconductors, telecommunications equipment, industrial machinery, and many of the other physical inputs required for the AI investment buildout. This fits directly with the manufacturing and capacity data discussed in our recent work. U.S. companies are attempting to deploy extraordinary amounts of capital into data centers, compute, networking, power infrastructure, and related equipment, but domestic production cannot satisfy all of that demand. A portion of the investment boom therefore leaks into imports.

That creates an unusual GDP accounting paradox. The stronger U.S. investment demand becomes, the more capital equipment businesses may need to import. Those imports worsen the trade balance and subtract from headline GDP even though the economic reason they are rising is precisely because domestic businesses are spending aggressively. If the current trade pattern persists, net exports could become a meaningful drag on third-quarter GDP while underlying private demand remains substantially stronger than the headline growth rate implies.

The sequencing can therefore look something like this:

AI investment accelerates → demand for capital equipment rises → domestic supply cannot fully respond → capital-goods imports surge → the trade deficit widens → net exports subtract from GDP → headline GDP understates the strength of domestic investment demand.

That is fundamentally different from a trade deficit widening because U.S. production and exports are collapsing alongside weak domestic demand. Both scenarios subtract from GDP through the same accounting identity, but they carry very different information about the business cycle. A softer GDP print caused by imported GPUs, semiconductors, electrical equipment, and industrial machinery should not be interpreted the same way as a softer GDP print caused by collapsing consumption or business investment.

The 4.2% growth rate in Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers is therefore particularly important. It reinforces the broader two-speed economy we have been discussing. Housing remains constrained, portions of the consumer remain sensitive to affordability, and aggregate GDP growth can appear relatively subdued. Yet the private domestic economy is still absorbing substantial investment, manufacturing New Orders are expanding, capital-spending expectations remain exceptionally strong, and corporations continue importing the equipment required to expand productive capacity.

There is also an important inflation implication. The widening trade deficit is effectively demonstrating that part of the AI investment boom is outrunning the productive capacity currently available within the United States. Rather than simply bidding against one another for scarce domestic equipment, businesses are reaching overseas for additional supply. That helps expand the economy's future productive capacity, but in the near term it can also place upward pressure on capital-goods import prices, which have already accelerated materially. The investment boom is therefore simultaneously increasing future supply and creating current demand pressure.

This is another reason the Federal Reserve faces such an unusual reaction function. Headline GDP can slow enough to suggest the economy is losing momentum while the private-demand data underneath it remain too strong to provide a conventional recessionary signal. Labor can cool while manufacturing accelerates. Housing can contract while capital equipment imports surge. The economy increasingly cannot be summarized by a single aggregate growth number because the composition of that growth has become unusually important.

For markets, the distinction will matter considerably if third-quarter GDP comes in softer than expected. The first question should not be whether GDP slowed. It should be why it slowed. If the drag comes disproportionately from net exports because U.S. companies are importing enormous quantities of capital equipment while Real Final Sales to Private Domestic Purchasers remain strong, the underlying earnings and business-cycle message would be considerably healthier than the headline number suggests.

The trade deficit is widening, but in this instance part of that deterioration is a symptom of strength rather than weakness. The United States is importing more because the domestic investment cycle is demanding more equipment than the domestic economy can currently produce. That may depress measured GDP in the near term, but it simultaneously reinforces the larger theme running through this cycle: headline growth can look mediocre while the capital-intensive portion of the private economy remains extraordinarily strong.

Consumer Confidence

Households Are Fine Today, Worried About Tomorrow

The latest Conference Board Consumer Confidence report reinforces the growing divide between how households view the economy today and what they expect over the coming months. The headline index slipped to 89.4 in August from a downwardly revised 90.2 in July, but the composition was considerably more important. The Present Situation Index actually rose 6.8 points to 121.2, ending three consecutive monthly declines, while the Expectations Index fell another 5.8 points to 68.2, its lowest level since January.

The divergence below is the important signal. Consumers are not describing an economy that is currently in recession. Current labor-market perceptions actually improved, with 27.0% of respondents describing jobs as plentiful compared with 19.5% saying jobs were hard to get, leaving the jobs differential at a still-positive 7.5 percentage points. That fits with the broader labor data discussed throughout this report. Initial Claims remain low, state-level employment breadth has improved materially, and the broad firing cycle normally associated with recession has not developed.

What is deteriorating is confidence in what comes next. Expectations surrounding future business conditions, employment, and income weakened further, pushing the Expectations Index to 68.2. Historically, sustained weakness in expectations has often appeared around economic downturns, but the current cycle has repeatedly demonstrated why survey data should not be treated mechanically. The better interpretation is that households see current conditions holding together while becoming increasingly uncertain about whether that resilience can persist.

Housing intentions provide one of the clearest examples of that caution translating into behavior. Only 5.2% of consumers now expect to purchase a home over the next six months, down from 6.5% in July and the largest monthly decline in more than five years. That aligns with the housing data discussed above. Mortgage rates remain restrictive, Housing Starts are weakening, Pending Home Sales remain depressed, and the long end of the Treasury curve continues limiting any meaningful recovery in housing activity.

The distinction matters because expectations can eventually influence the hard data before unemployment materially rises. A household that becomes concerned about future employment or income can delay a home purchase, reduce discretionary spending, or increase precautionary savings without first losing a job. If that behavior becomes sufficiently broad, weaker expectations can eventually translate into weaker realized demand. The decline in home-buying intentions suggests that transmission is already visible in one of the economy's most rate-sensitive areas.

At the same time, the chart argues against making a broad recession call today. The Present Situation Index remains substantially above Expectations, current labor perceptions improved, state employment breadth is recovering, and private domestic demand remains resilient. Manufacturing and capital spending are also providing an important offset to weakness across housing and portions of the consumer.

The question is therefore which side of the chart ultimately converges toward the other. The constructive outcome is that employment remains stable and expectations eventually recover toward still-resilient current conditions. The more concerning outcome is that consumers are correctly anticipating deterioration that has not yet reached the coincident data, with weaker expectations eventually feeding into spending, employment, and the Present Situation Index itself.

For now, consumers are not saying the economy is bad today. They are increasingly questioning whether today's conditions can last.

Income Quality

Transfers Are Doing More of the Work

The July personal income data initially look relatively constructive. Personal income increased 0.4% month over month, disposable personal income rose 0.5%, and real disposable income increased 0.4%. At the same time, the personal savings rate increased to 3.0% from 2.6% in June. We will address the inflation side of the report separately below, but the income composition deserves considerably more attention because the headline numbers increasingly overstate the strength of income being generated organically by the private economy.

The important distinction is between total personal income and personal income excluding government transfer payments. Transfer payments now represent roughly 19% of personal income, meaning an increasingly significant portion of aggregate household cash flow comes from Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid-related transfers, unemployment benefits, and other government programs rather than wages, proprietors' income, interest, dividends, or other market-generated sources. More importantly, real personal income excluding transfers, one of the measures included within the indicators historically monitored by the NBER when assessing the business cycle, has now been negative year over year for five consecutive months. Headline household income is still rising, but the underlying income generated before government transfers is considerably weaker.

That distinction matters most for the lower half of the K-shaped economy. Higher-income households continue receiving an important offset through financial assets, interest income, and accumulated wealth, while households with fewer assets remain substantially more dependent on wages and transfer income to support consumption. The fact that real disposable income increased while underlying income excluding transfers remains weak therefore helps explain how aggregate consumption can continue holding together even as portions of the consumer report considerably greater financial stress. Transfers can stabilize household cash flow, but they do not provide the same cyclical signal as rising private-sector labor and business income.

The increase in the savings rate from 2.6% to 3.0% is also worth monitoring. A higher savings rate is healthy from a household balance-sheet perspective, particularly after several years in which consumers relied on unusually low savings to absorb higher prices. From the perspective of near-term economic growth, however, savings and consumption compete for the same incremental dollar of income. If households become more cautious and rebuild savings rather than spend, consumption growth can slow even without an outright decline in employment or income. That appears relevant in July, when current-dollar spending increased only 0.2% and real consumption was essentially unchanged.

Higher yields reinforce that mechanism. One channel through which restrictive interest rates slow economic activity is by increasing the return available on cash, money-market funds, CDs, and other savings vehicles. The greater the compensation households receive for postponing consumption, the more attractive saving becomes at the margin. That can support interest income for asset-owning households, but it simultaneously raises the hurdle for current spending and investment. In an economy where consumption represents the majority of GDP, even a modest shift from spending toward saving can become meaningful if it persists.

For now, the income data are not signaling a collapse in the consumer. Real disposable income increased and the labor market continues to provide a meaningful floor beneath household cash flow. But the composition is becoming less constructive than the headline suggests. Transfer payments are playing an increasingly important stabilizing role, real income excluding transfers has been contracting year over year, and households are beginning to retain a larger portion of their income rather than immediately spend it. That combination reinforces the broader picture of a consumer that remains functional, but increasingly cautious, with the lower half of the K carrying considerably less internally generated income momentum than the aggregate data imply.

Labor Supply

Payroll Momentum Is Stalling as Participation Falls

The labor market continues to be characterized by policymakers as strong, but the better description increasingly looks like stable and stagnant. Payroll growth has slowed dramatically without producing the corresponding increase in unemployment that would normally accompany that deterioration. The 12-month average monthly payroll gain shown below has fallen to just 32K, yet the unemployment rate remains historically low. That combination is possible because labor supply is contracting alongside labor demand. Fewer workers are entering or remaining in the labor force, which lowers the pace of job creation required to keep unemployment from rising. The Fed can therefore point to a low unemployment rate as evidence of labor-market strength even while the underlying employment engine is producing very little incremental job growth.

The decline in participation among workers aged 55 and older is particularly important. The year-over-year change in the 55+ labor-force participation rate has fallen roughly 1.1 percentage points, one of the sharpest declines outside the pandemic period. Part of that likely reflects demographics, but the wealth effect may also be contributing. Home values and financial assets have appreciated substantially throughout this cycle, leaving many older households with stronger balance sheets and greater flexibility to retire earlier than they otherwise would. Rising asset prices can therefore tighten measured labor supply by allowing older workers to permanently exit the workforce. That helps keep unemployment contained even as payroll creation slows because those individuals are no longer counted as unemployed once they stop actively looking for work.

There is a similar but economically different participation issue developing among younger workers. Labor-force participation among the 18-to-24-year-old cohort has also weakened while hiring rates remain depressed and entry-level employment has become increasingly difficult to secure. AI is unlikely to explain that entire deterioration, but it may be contributing at the margin because many of the tasks most exposed to automation sit within the junior white-collar positions traditionally used to bring younger workers into the labor market. The combination of slower hiring, fewer entry-level opportunities, and businesses increasingly focused on extracting more output from existing employees can discourage younger workers from entering or remaining in the labor force.

The BLS's new 2025–2035 employment projections provide an important longer-term framework for that possibility. Total employment is projected to increase by only 5.9 million jobs, or 3.5%, over the coming decade, substantially slower than the 10.9% expansion recorded between 2015 and 2025. At the same time, the composition is expected to shift materially. Computing infrastructure, data processing, power generation, and electrical equipment are projected to benefit from the AI investment boom, while Office and Administrative Support employment is projected to decline by roughly 752K jobs. Data Scientists and Computer and Information Research Scientists, by contrast, are expected to experience substantial employment growth. AI can therefore increase investment, electricity consumption, productive capacity, and economic output while simultaneously reducing the labor intensity of portions of the economy.

That distinction may become increasingly important for how we interpret payroll data. Historically, strong economic growth required businesses to continually add workers because producing more output generally required more labor. If AI allows companies to generate more revenue and output with fewer incremental employees, payroll growth can remain structurally weaker without necessarily implying equally weak GDP or corporate earnings. The manufacturing and investment data discussed throughout this report already hint at that possibility. Capital spending and New Orders remain strong while aggregate hiring has slowed substantially.

The recent BLS benchmark revision also reduces the concern that today's weak payroll picture is simply another measurement problem. The preliminary March 2026 benchmark revision lowered total Nonfarm Payrolls by only 79K, or 0.1%, and private employment by 178K, also roughly 0.1%. That is dramatically smaller than the 862K downward revision incorporated for the year through March 2025. Payroll growth is weak today because hiring has genuinely slowed, not because the establishment survey appears to be hiding another enormous level error.

The chart below therefore captures an important structural feature of the current labor market. Payroll momentum is approaching stall speed, but declining participation is simultaneously lowering the number of jobs required to keep unemployment stable. Older workers may increasingly be leaving because accumulated wealth gives them the ability to retire, while younger workers face a labor market where entry has become more difficult as hiring slows and technology changes the demand for junior labor.

That is why describing the labor market simply as "strong" increasingly misses what is happening underneath the headline unemployment rate. It is not collapsing, because layoffs remain contained and labor supply is contracting alongside labor demand. But it is not particularly dynamic either. The labor market increasingly looks less like one characterized by strong hiring and more like one where fewer people are looking for work at the same time businesses need fewer incremental workers.

For the Fed and Kevin Warsh, that distinction matters. A low unemployment rate still provides room to focus on inflation, but it should not be confused with an accelerating labor market. If participation continues falling while payroll growth remains near current levels, the unemployment rate can remain deceptively stable even as the underlying labor market becomes progressively less dynamic. The next question is therefore not simply whether unemployment rises. It is whether productivity and shrinking labor supply can allow the economy to continue growing with structurally less job creation than investors and policymakers have historically considered normal.

Inflation Test

Warsh's Burden of Proof Is Disinflation

The July PCE report did little to strengthen the argument that inflation is naturally converging back toward the Federal Reserve's target. Headline PCE increased 0.2% month over month and remained 3.7% year over year, while Core PCE also increased 0.2% and remained 3.3% above last year. The monthly numbers are not alarming in isolation, but they are also not particularly reassuring after more than five years of inflation remaining above the Fed's 2% objective. More importantly, the shorter-term trend continues running hotter than the year-over-year rate. As shown below, six-month annualized headline PCE is running at 4.1% compared with 3.7% year over year. Inflation is therefore not simply above target. The more recent rate of change remains above the trailing twelve-month pace.

That distinction sits directly at the center of Kevin Warsh's emerging reaction function. At Jackson Hole, Warsh reiterated that the Fed's 2% PCE objective is "firm" and "fixed" and pushed back against the assumption that inflation will automatically mean-revert toward target. His standard was relatively straightforward: policymakers need to see underlying inflation moving toward 2% clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, in his words, the Fed still has work to do. July did not provide that confirmation. The report was not an inflation breakout, but neither did it satisfy the increasingly important requirement for continued disinflation.

The breadth of inflation reinforces that concern. Warsh highlighted that roughly 54% of PCE components are still increasing more than 3% year over year, compared with approximately 32% during the two decades before the pandemic. That matters because the Fed can more easily look through an isolated energy or commodity shock than inflation that remains distributed across a large portion of the consumption basket. Oil and geopolitical disruptions continue creating headline volatility, but the persistence underneath those categories makes it more difficult to argue that the remaining inflation problem is entirely supply-driven.

What makes the policy debate more complicated is that Warsh simultaneously described an economy that looks considerably stronger than several traditional leading indicators suggest. Equipment and intangible investment are growing around 9% over four quarters, more than half of this year's capex growth is tied to AI, private domestic demand remains firm, corporate profits are strong, credit spreads remain tight, issuance is healthy, and bank lending standards are relatively easy. His conclusion was important: it is difficult to characterize broad financial conditions as particularly restrictive simply because housing and other rate-sensitive sectors are struggling.

That fits directly with the two-speed economy discussed throughout our research. Housing is clearly responding to elevated long-term rates, and portions of the consumer are becoming increasingly cautious. Yet the capital-intensive side of the economy continues expanding rapidly enough to support private demand, manufacturing, corporate profits, and financial markets. The Fed is therefore unlikely to respond to weakness in an individual rate-sensitive sector if aggregate demand remains resilient and inflation continues running above target.

The chart below makes the problem particularly clear. If the six-month annualized inflation rate were falling materially beneath the year-over-year measure, the Fed could reasonably argue that the lagging twelve-month number was overstating current inflation pressure. Today, the opposite is true. Six-month annualized PCE at 4.1% is running above the 3.7% year-over-year rate. The recent direction of inflation therefore provides considerably less comfort than the simple observation that inflation is well below its 2022 peak.

This also explains why September has become a genuinely live meeting. Warsh did not promise a hike and has explicitly rejected the type of forward guidance that characterized previous Fed regimes. Instead, he appears intent on restoring optionality by forcing markets to respond to incoming data rather than a pre-communicated policy path. That makes every inflation report more consequential because investors can no longer assume the Fed will telegraph its next move several meetings in advance.

The market reaction to Jackson Hole reflected that adjustment. The front end repriced toward a materially greater probability of a September hike, the dollar strengthened, and gold weakened as investors recognized that tightening optionality had not been fully reflected in asset prices. Importantly, equities remained relatively resilient, which itself supports part of Warsh's argument. If financial markets can absorb higher expected policy rates without meaningful deterioration in credit or equity conditions, the Fed has less reason to believe current policy is imposing excessive restraint on aggregate demand.

There is also an important tension developing between the Fed and the long end of the Treasury curve. Treasury has become increasingly active in supporting market functioning as long yields move into economically uncomfortable territory, while Warsh continues emphasizing the importance of allowing market prices to provide relatively unfiltered information about financial conditions. He has not directly criticized Treasury's actions, but the institutional distinction matters. Treasury increasingly wants relief from long-term financing costs, while the Fed is signaling that persistent inflation may still require additional restraint at the front end.

That leaves the policy configuration unusually complicated. Housing would benefit from lower rates. The consumer would benefit from lower financing costs. Treasury would prefer less pressure at the long end. But manufacturing, AI investment, corporate earnings, and private domestic demand remain strong enough that the Fed cannot simply respond to those weaker sectors while inflation is still running above target and the shorter-term inflation trend remains elevated.

For Warsh, the burden of proof therefore appears to have shifted. The question is no longer whether the economy is weak enough to justify leaving rates unchanged. It is whether inflation is improving quickly enough to justify not tightening further.

July PCE did not answer that question decisively, but it moved the data in the wrong direction. With year-over-year PCE at 3.7%, six-month annualized inflation at 4.1%, and underlying economic activity remaining resilient, September is now a live hike meeting precisely because the Fed is no longer willing to assume that time alone will finish the inflation fight.

Policy Credibility

Gold and Bitcoin Are Hedging the Limits of Restraint

The final chart may be the cleanest way to tie together the cross-asset message running through this report. Gold and Bitcoin are increasingly trading as expressions of the same macro concern, with their rolling 90-day correlation rising to roughly 0.49, near the highest levels since 2021. That is notable because the traditional monetary backdrop should not be particularly supportive for either asset. Real yields remain historically elevated, with the 10-year real rate near the upper end of its past-decade distribution, while the Fed is openly debating another rate hike. Under the conventional framework, a higher real return on risk-free government debt should increase the opportunity cost of owning assets that produce no contractual cash flow.

Yet both are rising anyway.

That tells us the market is increasingly responding to something beyond the expected path of short-term rates. The catalyst for the latest move was Treasury's decision to expand long-end buybacks, which triggered a sharp reversal in yields and the dollar and immediately benefited gold, miners, and Bitcoin. But the larger issue is what that intervention represented. After the 30-year Treasury moved above 5% and term premium approached historical extremes, policymakers demonstrated that there is a level of long-term financing costs they are increasingly uncomfortable allowing the market to reach without some response.

The problem is that the underlying reasons long yields are rising have not disappeared. Fiscal deficits remain extraordinarily large, Treasury must continue issuing enormous amounts of debt, foreign investors are increasingly favoring U.S. equities over duration, inflation has remained above the Fed's target for more than five years, and the capital spending cycle continues supporting nominal growth. Bond investors are therefore demanding greater compensation to absorb duration at precisely the moment policymakers would prefer lower long-term financing costs.

That tension increasingly resembles a credibility problem rather than simply a rates problem. If bond vigilantes continue pushing long yields higher because the fiscal and inflation outlook requires greater compensation, policymakers eventually face an uncomfortable choice. They can allow yields to rise until private demand clears the enormous supply of debt, accepting the resulting pressure on housing, the consumer, federal interest expense, and asset valuations. Or they can intervene more aggressively to suppress long-term financing costs, risking a larger adjustment through the currency, inflation expectations, and hard assets instead.

Gold and Bitcoin appear increasingly sensitive to that second possibility.

This does not mean the two assets are economically identical. Gold has thousands of years of monetary history, significant central-bank ownership, and a much lower volatility profile. Bitcoin remains a younger, more speculative asset with substantially greater sensitivity to liquidity and risk appetite. But both sit outside the traditional sovereign liability structure. Neither represents a claim on government cash flows, and both have relatively constrained supply compared with the ability of governments to issue additional nominal liabilities. When concerns shift from the level of interest rates toward the credibility of the system determining those rates, the commonality between the two becomes more important.

That may explain why their correlation is rising at the same time their traditional relationship with real yields is becoming less reliable. Investors are not necessarily buying Gold and Bitcoin because monetary policy is easy today. They may be buying them because the combination of persistent deficits, enormous refinancing requirements, above-target inflation, rising term premium, and increasing policy sensitivity to long-end yields raises questions about how restrictive policymakers can ultimately allow financial conditions to become.

Warsh's more hawkish reaction function complicates that thesis in the near term. A credible Fed willing to raise rates despite political and market pressure could strengthen the dollar, contain inflation expectations, and temporarily pressure both assets. In fact, that may be exactly why restoring Fed credibility matters so much. But the Fed controls the overnight rate more directly than it controls the fiscal trajectory or the compensation private investors demand for holding 10- and 30-year government debt. A tighter front end cannot independently solve a structural fiscal imbalance.

This is ultimately the tension the market appears to be pricing. The Fed is attempting to restore inflation credibility while Treasury is becoming increasingly sensitive to the consequences of elevated long-term yields. The government needs enormous amounts of financing, bond investors want greater compensation to provide it, and rate-sensitive portions of the economy are already struggling with the yields required to clear that supply.

For now, credit spreads and volatility continue to argue against interpreting this as an imminent sovereign or financial crisis. The Treasury market is functioning, foreign capital continues flowing aggressively into U.S. assets, and equities remain near record highs. But Gold and Bitcoin are increasingly telling us that investors are beginning to hedge a different tail risk.

The risk is not simply that rates go higher.

It is that policymakers eventually decide they cannot allow them to.

That is the neat bow connecting the dollar, Treasury buybacks, rising term premium, persistent fiscal deficits, and the simultaneous strength in Gold and Bitcoin. Real yields are near historical extremes, yet alternative monetary assets are rising together anyway. The market may increasingly be pricing not today's monetary restraint, but the limits of how long that restraint can be maintained when the sovereign itself is one of the largest borrowers exposed to it.

Bottom Line

The Adjustment Is About Composition

The data continue to describe an economy undergoing a change in composition rather than a conventional synchronized slowdown. Headline GDP can look weak because surging capital-goods imports subtract through net exports while underlying private domestic demand remains strong. Payroll growth can approach stall speed without unemployment rising because labor-force participation is contracting alongside hiring. Consumers can remain employed while simultaneously becoming more cautious about future income and increasing savings. None of those divergences is inherently recessionary, but together they make the aggregate statistics increasingly difficult to interpret without understanding what is happening beneath them.

The central macro tension remains that the economy is becoming more capital intensive and potentially less labor intensive. AI investment is supporting equipment demand, manufacturing, infrastructure, electricity consumption, productivity, profits, and imports while potentially allowing businesses to produce more output with fewer incremental workers. If that transition persists, the historical relationship between payroll growth and economic strength may become less reliable. The economy may simply require fewer new workers to generate the same amount of incremental output.

For the Fed, however, that is not automatically a dovish development. Stronger productivity may eventually increase potential growth and reduce inflation, but the investment required to create that capacity is generating significant demand today. With six-month annualized PCE still running above the year-over-year rate and private domestic demand remaining resilient, Warsh has made clear that the burden of proof increasingly sits with disinflation. The Fed does not need to hike simply because inflation remains above 2%, but it is no longer willing to assume that time alone will finish the job.

That creates the most important policy tension in the current regime. The Fed may need to preserve or increase restraint to restore inflation credibility while Treasury increasingly wants relief from the long-term yields produced by persistent deficits, enormous financing requirements, inflation uncertainty, and elevated term premium. Those objectives can coexist temporarily, but they become increasingly difficult to reconcile if bond investors continue demanding greater compensation for duration.

The simultaneous strength in Gold and Bitcoin may be the market's early expression of that conflict. Neither asset should find historically elevated real yields particularly supportive, yet their correlation has risen toward its highest level since 2021 while both move higher. Investors may increasingly be hedging not against monetary easing today, but against the possibility that policymakers eventually become unwilling to tolerate the long-term financing costs required to clear the sovereign debt market without intervention.

That remains a tail risk rather than our base case. Credit spreads remain contained, equity markets remain resilient, Treasury markets continue functioning, and foreign capital continues flowing into U.S. assets. There is no evidence today of a systemic funding crisis. The more appropriate interpretation is that the market is beginning to assign a larger premium to fiscal and policy credibility alongside the traditional growth and inflation risks.

The next phase therefore comes down to which adjustment occurs first. Inflation can moderate enough to give the Fed room to ease without sacrificing credibility. Productivity can accelerate enough to convert today's AI demand shock into tomorrow's supply expansion. Or long-term yields can continue rising until policymakers are forced to decide how much market-based tightening they are actually willing to tolerate.

For now, the economy remains strong enough to keep that decision from becoming urgent, but uneven enough that the cost of getting it wrong is rising. The most important signal is no longer simply whether growth accelerates or slows. It is whether the investment boom can expand productive capacity faster than inflation, fiscal pressure, and long-term financing costs tighten around it.
